title: Multi-Agent Coordination Adaptation via Structure-Guided Orchestration
summary: MACA addresses a tension in LLM-based multi-agent systems between structural stability and dynamic adaptability. Structure-centric methods fix a topology before execution, which limits adaptation as task states change, while orchestration-centric methods adapt step by step but leave coordination structure implicit, producing high-variance coordination as the number of agents grows. MACA treats coordination as posterior inference over the joint distribution of structure and orchestration. It learns a task- and budget-conditioned structural prior, called GraphSpec, that scores agent relevance and interaction plausibility to form a probabilistic interaction graph constraining agent participation and information flow. A token-aware orchestration policy then selects agents step by step within this reduced space, with the prior acting as a constraint through reward modulation. Agents come from a predefined pool with manually specified capabilities and role descriptions, such as planner, coder, tester, and documenter. Across six benchmarks, MACA outperforms adaptive multi-agent baselines by an average of 8.42% while using 43.19% fewer tokens, and joint adaptation reportedly suppresses redundant interactions. The authors note several limitations. Evaluation centers on relatively structured benchmarks, so generalization to open-ended or domain-specific settings is not established. Part of the gains may stem from careful agent initialization rather than coordination alone. GraphSpec is trained on filtered high-quality trajectories and final-outcome supervision, which may favor easily verifiable patterns and reduce robustness where credit assignment is noisy or intermediate collaboration matters.
